title: Affordance
body:
An **affordance** is a possibility for action offered by an object to a particular user. A
handle affords pulling, a flat plate affords pushing, a chair affords sitting for an adult and
climbing for a small child.

The affordance is a relationship between the object and the user, so it exists whether or not
anybody notices it. What the user actually perceives is the [[Signifier]], and separating the
two is the point of the concept.

```
a door with a handle on the push side

  affords:     pushing, since it is hinged to swing that way
  signifies:   pulling, since a handle is what you pull
  result:      the user pulls, the door stays shut, and the user feels stupid
```

That mismatch is the standard example of the entire topic, and the diagnosis is that the design
failed, and the person who walked into the door did nothing wrong. Adding a sign reading PUSH
is the admission of failure: the object should communicate its use without instructions.

In software the affordances are entirely constructed, since nothing on a screen physically
affords anything, which makes signifiers the whole game. A raised rectangle with a label
signifies a button, and removing the visual difference in the name of clean design removes the
signal that it can be pressed.
